role: Self-test of the six kernels of bandwidth.c. Not run in the 2026-11-17 rerun.
purpose: selftest.c calls the six kernels of bandwidth.c (the new benchmark source) on small buffers (at most 1 MiB) and checks the memory afterwards. run_kernels.sh (the script of 2026-11-13) built it and ran it before its own timed runs, and it does not run during the rerun of 2026-11-17.

main_flow.step: The compiler copies the text of bandwidth.c into this file. So the test calls the kernels of the benchmark source, not copies of them.
The program takes no arguments and reads no environment variable. `main` makes the output line-buffered, reads the page size and prints the header line.
For 3 buffer sizes (1 page, 3 pages, 1 MiB) `test_size` checks the C kernels, then the asm kernels, each over a whole buffer between two guard pages.
For 2 block positions (page start, page end) `test_block` checks one 256 B loop pass of the C kernels, then of the asm kernels.
`main` prints the number of failed checks and returns exit status 0 (every check passed) or 1.

behavior_notes: This file times nothing. It reads no clock and prints no rate.

It does not run during the rerun of 2026-11-17. That rerun builds nothing. ra.sh uses the binaries bw_old and bw_new of 2026-11-13. None of the four scripts of the rerun (go.sh, go2.sh, ra.sh, rx.sh) names this file [Ref5].

It tests bandwidth.c only. That is the source of bw_new, which holds the new read kernel. It does not test bandwidth.orig.c (the source of bw_old). The old read kernel is therefore not covered [Ref1].
The runner bwx12 has its own self-test in another file, bwx12_selftest.c [Ref7].

Limits, from the file header: the test sees memory contents and faults only. A read kernel that loads nothing would pass. The machine code listing in probe.txt is the evidence that `k_read` and `k_asmread` of bw_new load 256 B per loop pass, with 8 `ldp` instructions of 32 B each [Ref3].

Insufficient data: whether the kernels inside the selftest binary have the same machine code as the kernels inside bw_new. An objdump listing of the selftest binary would resolve it. The selftest binary is not in the local folders. Both binaries are built from the same bandwidth.c with the same flags. They are separate compilations. probe.txt holds listings of the kernels of bw_new and bw_old. It holds no listing of the selftest binary [Ref1] [Ref3].
Exit status: 0 = every check passed. 1 = at least one check failed. 2 = setup failed (`mmap`, `mprotect`, or a page size that is not a multiple of 256 B).

A kernel that reads or writes a guard page ends the process with `SIGSEGV`. Then the output has no `# failures=` line, and its last `call,` line names the kernel. The shell reports exit status 139 (128 plus the signal number 11).
run_kernels.sh ends with exit status 4 when the self-test does not return 0. So it timed no kernel on 2026-11-13 before the self-test had passed [Ref1].

Result of 2026-11-13: page size 4096 bytes, 30 `call` lines, 36 result lines, all `pass`, last line `# failures=0`. The results folder holds three runs of run_kernels.sh from that day (18:12:10, 18:12:22 and 18:32:18 UTC). The three selftest.txt files (the saved output of the self-test, one file per run) have the same sha256 value [Ref2]. Only the run of 18:12:22 had the mode `all` (the mode with timed runs). The other two had the mode `probe` (build, machine code and self-test, no timed runs) [Ref4].

The selftest binary had the same sha256 value in the three builds of 2026-11-13 that the results folder records (it starts with 80714eb8). The sha256 value of bandwidth.c differs between the second build (c1406e02) and the third build (f1985072). So that change of bandwidth.c did not change the selftest binary. The bandwidth.c in this folder is the text of the third build. The selftest.c in this folder is the text of these three builds (90456a56) [Ref4].

The first build also recorded c1406e02 for bandwidth.c. The second build (18:12:22 UTC) is the one with the timed runs. So the self-test that ran before the timed runs was built from a text of bandwidth.c that is not the text in this folder. The binary bw_new also had the same sha256 value in the three builds (it starts with fd7c14df) [Ref4]. The two texts differ in comment lines only. An edit of 2026-11-13 18:32:07 UTC replaced 2 comment lines above `k_read` with the 5 comment lines 178 to 182 of the local text [Ref8]. With this edit reversed, the local text has the sha256 value of the earlier text (c1406e02...). No code line differs.

words.def: the Arm reference server under test. It has 128 CPUs.
an inner loop of the benchmark that reads, writes or copies memory. It never means the Linux kernel. The operating system kernel is always written "Linux kernel".

the C kernels are `k_read`, `k_write` and `k_copy`, written with NEON intrinsics. The asm kernels are `k_asmread`, `k_asmwrite` and `k_asmcopy`, written as inline assembly. All six are functions of bandwidth.c.
NEON intrinsics (C functions that map to Arm vector instructions), loads only. Its name is `read` in the binary bw_new and `read` in bwx12.
portable C code with 16 running sums. Each load is followed by an add. Its name is `read` in the binary bw_old and `oldread` in the runner bwx12.
the benchmark and its two binaries of 2026-11-13. bw_old was built from the old source, bw_new from the new source.
later runner programs for the same loops. They print one row per thread. bwx12 is the runner of the 2026-11-15 investigation. bwx11 and bwx are older versions.
one unsigned 64-bit integer (8 bytes). The kernels take the buffer length as a count of words.
one run of the loop body of a kernel. Each kernel of bandwidth.c moves 256 B (32 words) per loop pass.
the unit in which the Linux kernel manages memory. One page had 4096 bytes on CRB in this test.
a page with the protection `PROT_NONE` (no access allowed), placed directly before or directly after a test buffer. A read or a write of it ends the process with the signal `SIGSEGV`.
the second argument of `pattern`. The four fill loops of selftest.c use the numbers 1 to 4, so no two fills give a word the same value.
here "ldp q", the Arm instruction that loads two 16-byte vector registers (32 B).
the script of 2026-11-13. It built bw_old, bw_new and the self-test, compiled probe.c, printed the machine code of the kernels and ran the self-test. In its mode `all` it then timed the kernels.

a text file that run_kernels.sh wrote into its result folder. It holds the compiler, the flags, the sha256 values, the machine code of the kernels and the exit status of the self-test. During the rerun ra.sh writes another file with the same name into its own result folder. That file holds no machine code.
the tool that prints the machine code of a binary as text.
a checksum of a file. Two files with the same sha256 value have the same content.
the test under review: the 120-thread read test on CRB after the memory speed was lowered. Its scripts are go.sh, go2.sh, ra.sh and rx.sh.
our runs use CPUs 0-119 only: 64 threads on mesh 0 plus 56 threads on mesh 1. Each thread reads its own buffer of 256 MiB from memory.
the two halves of the chip. CPUs 0-63 sit on mesh 0. CPUs 64-127 sit on mesh 1.

functions.name: guarded
functions.what: Maps a buffer of n words with one no-access page before it and one after it. Exits with status 2 on failure.

functions.name: pattern
functions.what: Returns the test value of word i for one salt. Different indexes give different values.

functions.name: calling
functions.what: Prints the line "call,kernel,bytes" before a kernel call.

functions.name: check
functions.what: Prints one result line with pass or FAIL. Counts a failed check in failures.

functions.name: test_size
functions.what: Checks one read, one write and one copy kernel over a whole guarded buffer of n words.

functions.name: test_block
functions.what: Checks one 256 B loop pass of each kernel at a word offset inside one guarded page.

functions.name: main
functions.what: Sets line buffering, reads the page size, runs test_size for 3 sizes and test_block for 2 offsets. Returns 0 when every check passed.
